messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Henry, a 62-year-old potter from a small town in North America, had lived a life filled with creativity and craftsmanship, but in recent years, shadows had begun to creep into his vibrant world. The unexpected death of his younger brother, Mark, two years ago, had shattered the once-sturdy foundation of his daily existence. Mark had been more than just a sibling; he was Henry’s confidant, the one who shared his passion for pottery and the joys of life. The way Henry remembered that fateful day was seared into his mind: he had received the call while working in his studio, the sudden news striking him like a violent wave. As he stood there, surrounded by his clay and tools, the world around him faded, leaving only the harsh reality of loss.

In the months that followed, Henry found himself grappling with a torrent of emotions, yet he felt compelled to push them away. Whenever a flicker of joy would surface, whether it was the laughter of children playing outside or a tender moment shared with his wife, he would suppress it, convinced that allowing any happiness would feel like a betrayal to Mark’s memory. It had become an instinctual response; positive emotions felt unsafe, as if they could shatter the fragile peace he had managed to establish in his heart. This avoidance of positive feelings extended to every aspect of his life, as he believed that embracing joy now would only amplify the pain of loss.

Henry's avoidance strategies grew more pronounced as time went on. Anything that reminded him of Mark was swiftly pushed aside—photographs, shared music, or even the old pottery pieces they had worked on together. He kept the studio meticulously organized, but the absence of his brother’s presence was a gaping void. Even innocuous conversations about family gatherings or upcoming events would send him into a protective shell; he had learned to dodge any mention of the future, convinced that making plans would only lead to more heartache. The idea of a family reunion or a trip seemed unbearable, as he feared that such anticipations would only highlight the absence of his brother and the emptiness it created.

As days turned into months, Henry's studio, once a sanctuary of creation, became increasingly isolating. His wife, Clara, noticed the changes and tried to coax him into discussing his feelings, but every time she brought up Mark or suggested they plan a future trip, he would become withdrawn. The very thought of facing those emotions was daunting, and he could not shake the belief that confronting his grief would overwhelm him. He was convinced that the pain would engulf him completely, leaving nothing but desolation in its wake. This fear of emotional vulnerability led him to retreat further into solitude, creating an invisible barrier between himself and the world.

At night, Henry often sat in silence, the weight of his loss pressing down on him like a stone. He would stare at the moonlight spilling across the floor of his studio, a stark reminder of the joy he once shared with Mark, and the laughter that now felt like a distant memory. Though there were fleeting moments when he thought of seeking help, the thought was quickly dismissed. He had come to believe that he could handle this alone, that opening up would only deepen his wounds. Yet, as the months dragged on, he felt more like a shell of his former self, trapped in a cycle of avoidance and grief.

Eventually, it was a quiet evening, sitting with Clara, that the dam began to crack. She spoke softly about wanting to take a weekend trip to the beach, a place they had once enjoyed together. Henry felt a surge of panic rise within him, but this time, instead of withdrawing, he found himself voicing his fears. “What if it hurts too much?” he confessed, the words tumbling out in a rush. Clara nodded, understanding the weight behind his question. It was in that small moment of vulnerability that Henry realized he could no longer navigate this pain by himself. Seeking help had become an option he could no longer ignore, and with it came a glimmer of hope—perhaps it was possible to find a way back to joy, even in the shadow of loss.
